facts.text: British legend, not game canon: in Geoffrey of Monmouth, Merlin's craft gives Uther the likeness of Gorlois so that he lies with Igerna at Tintagel and Arthur is begotten; Uther is buried within the Giants' Dance.
Uther's restlessness over Tintagel, the borrowed face he still wears, the priestesses' washing as an answer to it, the templars' three nights and Loremaster Alain's note are Living Server writing.

story:
The chroniclers of Camelot bury Uther Pendragon inside the Giants' Dance, below his brother Ambrosius, in a chamber cut for him under the west halls, and they say he was laid there in his harness with the banner of the dragon of fire he took his name from. They do not say that he did not lie quiet. The barrow-keepers of the Plains say he never once has.

What troubles him, the Church at Old Sarum has always said, is Tintagel. On the night his son was begotten, Uther came to Igerna, Gorlois's wife, wearing Gorlois's face, which Merlin had lent him, while Gorlois was dying on the field; and out of that night came Arthur, and out of Arthur came the realm. The Church says Uther cannot rest because the realm was made out of a lie and he knows it. The minstrels say he cannot rest because he never once regretted it. Loremaster Alain of the Academy, who sends the realm's young down to lay him, says the shade still wears the borrowed face, and that anyone who comes close enough to see it will not be able to say afterwards whose it was.

Above his chamber, in the west halls, two priestesses of Coventina keep a well and pour its water down onto the floor, and the floor takes it, and it drips into the king's chamber below. They say they keep the chamber washed. The Church says they are washing the face off him, a little every day, and that when it is gone he will rest. The priestesses do not come down to him and he does not go up to them. He has nobody in the barrows. His brother is restless in his own hall to the west, and the dead of the Pendragon's household keep their own places, and when the old king is troubled, nothing comes.

He walks his chamber and does not leave it, and he does not look at the living until they are close enough to touch; then he looks, and draws. Templars came three nights running to defile his tomb, the barrow-keepers say, and were turned back each night by a king in borrowed harness who did not speak. The Academy's young lay him with the dust of a hollow man from Snowdonia, and he goes down, and before long he is walking his chamber again with the water dripping on him, because the face is not yet washed away.
legend: The Shade of Uther Pendragon is a level 55 ghost in his chamber directly under Coventina's well in the west halls of Stonehenge Barrows, the kill step of Symbol of the Broken (Dathmul's dust to Loremaster Alain first). He only notices you inside about 200 and has no faction, so nothing in the barrows comes to help him, and the two Priestesses of Purity above do not come down for him (they come as a pair if you fight THEM). No spells or styles in the data: a melee fight with a 55 with a little parry and evade, a group of fifties. Clear the spectral essences in his chamber first. He respawns in about five minutes.

aggro: You come into my chamber? Whose face do you see?

The Pendragon does not yield his tomb.

lairEntry: Water drips from the ceiling of a king's chamber.

loremasterTopic.text: Arthur's father, buried within the Giants' Dance in a chamber under the west halls of the [stonehenge barrows], who has never lain quiet. The Church says it is Tintagel: he came to Igerna wearing Gorlois's face, which Merlin lent him, and the shade wears it still. The priestesses of [coventina] pour their well water down on him; the Church says they are washing the face away. Nothing in the barrows comes to his aid.

bookPage: A note in the hand of Loremaster Alain of the Academy, left with the dust of the hollow man for the young the Academy sends to the barrows. When you reach the old king's chamber, look at his face before you strike, and then try to tell me whose it was. Nobody has yet. The priestesses above say they are washing it away; I asked them whose face, and they said the one he borrowed. I asked them whose he would have when it was gone. They said that is why they keep the well. Lay him with the dust. He will get up again. Every time he does, there is a little less of the borrowed face.
